literature.title: Opinion 36/2026 on the Proposal for a Regulation EU KIDS Act ('EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy')
literature.method: legislative opinion under Article 42(1) of Regulation 2018/1725
literature.headline: Strongly supports the aims and the privacy-preserving design of age assurance, but asks co-legislators to require age checks only where necessary and proportionate, to extend safety by design to all users, and to harmonise the GDPR age of consent for all online services.

literature.authors: O'Neill, B. (for the European Parliament, CULT Committee)
literature.title: The influence of social media on the development of children and young people
literature.venue: European Parliament, Policy Department for Structural and Cohesion Policies, PE 733.109, February 2023
literature.method: literature review of research on European children's social media use, plus legal and policy analysis of the EU framework
literature.outcomes: content, contact, conduct and contract risks; children's development, mental health and well-being
literature.headline: Children routinely meet harmful content, contacts, bullying and unfair commercial practices on social media, and recommender algorithms increase these risks; but the evidence of an overall positive or negative effect on children's mental health and well-being is mixed and inconclusive. Media literacy and supportive families and peers moderate the harm.
literature.summary_plain: A study for the European Parliament reviews what is known about how social media affect children: many documented risks, but no clear overall effect on mental health.
literature.citation: O'Neill, B. (for the European Parliament, CULT Committee) (2023), The influence of social media on the development of children and young people, European Parliament, Policy Department for Structural and Cohesion Policies, PE 733.109, February 2023

literature.authors: Office of the U.S. Surgeon General
literature.title: Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory (chapter: Social Media Has Both Positive and Negative Impacts on Children and Adolescents)
literature.venue: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services; NCBI Bookshelf NBK594763
literature.outcomes: youth mental health; benefits and harms of social media use
literature.headline: The advisory's chapter reviews the potential benefits of social media for children and adolescents (connection, support, self-expression) and its potential harms to their mental health, and concludes that the evidence is not yet sufficient to show that social media is safe for young people.
literature.summary_plain: The US Surgeon General's 2023 advisory weighs the benefits and harms of social media for young people's mental health.
literature.quality: Evidence review by a public health authority; not a study of EU law.

literature.authors: Gui, M., Respi, C., Abbiati, G., Paladini, C., Ercolanoni, S., Milzani, F., Pirola, T. & Vezzoli, G.
literature.title: Longitudinal effect of early social media use on standardized learning outcomes during school career
literature.method: difference-in-differences: 5,227 students in northern Italy, early adopters of social media (account created in grades 6-8) matched with late adopters (grade 9 or later), longitudinal standardised test scores
literature.outcomes: test scores in Italian, English and mathematics
literature.headline: Early social media use lowers learning outcomes in standardised tests among children aged 7-16; a substantial part of the effect runs through how pervasive smartphones are at key moments of the day.
literature.summary_plain: Italian children who got a social media account earlier did worse at school than those who started later.
literature.quality: Causal design (difference-in-differences with matching); one region; not a study of an EU law.
literature.citation: Gui, M., Respi, C., Abbiati, G., Paladini, C., Ercolanoni, S., Milzani, F., Pirola, T. & Vezzoli, G. (2026), Longitudinal effect of early social media use on standardized learning outcomes during school career, Nature Human Behaviour 10(10), 1953-1965

literature.authors: Broadhurst, K. A. and Webb, L. (Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology)
literature.title: Impacts of social media on children and young people
literature.method: evidence review produced in consultation with experts and stakeholders
literature.outcomes: mental and physical health, harassment and abuse, financial harms, behaviour, educational attainment; social connection, identity, learning and support
literature.headline: Research links social media use by children and young people both to benefits (friendship, identity, learning, access to support) and to harms (anxiety and depression, poor sleep, grooming and abuse, financial harms, lower attainment), but most studies are cross-sectional and short-term and cannot show causation; effects are often small or inconsistent. Platform safety-by-design, digital literacy and parental engagement may reduce the risks.
literature.summary_plain: The UK Parliament's science office reviews the evidence on how social media affect children: real benefits and risks, but weak evidence on cause and effect.
literature.quality: Evidence review; no new data. Notes major gaps: long-term effects, younger children, measures beyond time spent.
literature.verified: summary supplied by the site author (UK Parliament site blocks automated reading)
literature.citation: Broadhurst, K. A. and Webb, L. (2026), Impacts of social media on children and young people, POSTnote 780, Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology, UK Parliament

literature.authors: Köhler-Dauner, F., Peter, L., Sitarski, E., Chauviré-Geib, K., Haag, A.-C. and Fegert, J. M.
literature.title: Digital child protection in social networks: age verification and age-tiered regulation in Europe
literature.venue: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health 19, 143 (editorial)
literature.method: narrative review of research and of regulatory approaches in Europe, Australia, the UK and the US
literature.outcomes: circumvention of age limits, child protection, children's participation and rights
literature.headline: Argues that bans and age limits alone fail: studies from Norway, Australia, France and the US show children routinely get around them. Recommends a harmonised EU framework of privacy-preserving age verification combined with safety-by-design duties and media education, rather than access bans.
literature.summary_plain: Child psychiatrists argue that minimum ages for social media are easily evaded and that platform design and media education matter more.
literature.quality: Editorial review; no new data. Authors declare no competing interests and no external funding.
literature.verified: full text read (PMC, via NCBI E-utilities)
literature.citation: Köhler-Dauner, F., Peter, L., Sitarski, E., Chauviré-Geib, K., Haag, A.-C. and Fegert, J. M. (2025), Digital child protection in social networks: age verification and age-tiered regulation in Europe, Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health 19, 143, doi:10.1186/s13034-025-01016-x

literature.title: Online age verification methods for children
literature.venue: EPRS At a glance, PE 739.350, February 2023
literature.method: overview of age verification methods and platform practices
literature.outcomes: effectiveness of age verification, privacy and cybersecurity, digital skills
literature.headline: Reviews the main age verification methods, from self-declaration to biometrics and digital ID. Children bypass most of them; stronger methods raise privacy and cybersecurity risks; and there is no common EU guidance. Better digital skills for parents and children and child-friendly service design are also needed.
literature.summary_plain: Parliament's research service explains how websites check users' ages and why most checks are easy for children to get around.
literature.quality: Short policy overview; no new data.
literature.citation: Negreiro, M. (2023), Online age verification methods for children, EPRS At a glance, PE 739.350, European Parliament

literature.title: Age assurance practices of 50 online services used by children
literature.method: review of the published age policies and practices of online services used by children
literature.outcomes: age assurance at account creation, minimum ages, age-tiered safeguards
literature.headline: Finds large gaps in practice: very few of the services examined systematically check age when an account is created, and many check only in certain circumstances, if at all. Minimum ages tend to come from privacy or contract law rather than safety and vary by country; age-tiered safeguards can often be turned off or rely on parental controls.
literature.summary_plain: The OECD looked at how popular online services used by children check users' ages and found most rarely do.
literature.quality: Document review of company policies; no testing of whether the checks work.
literature.verified: abstract read (OpenAlex, Crossref doi:10.1787/a19853ab-en); OECD site blocks automated reading
literature.citation: OECD (2025), Age assurance practices of 50 online services used by children, OECD Publishing, Paris, doi:10.1787/a19853ab-en

literature.authors: Livingstone, S., Nair, A., Stoilova, M., van der Hof, S. and Caglar, C.
literature.title: Children's Rights and Online Age Assurance Systems: The Way Forward
literature.venue: The International Journal of Children's Rights 32(3), 721–747
literature.method: legal analysis of European age assurance requirements combined with social research on company compliance and family life
literature.outcomes: effectiveness of age assurance, children's rights (privacy, non-discrimination, participation, remedy)
literature.headline: Age assurance is often ineffective in protecting children from online harm, and as currently implemented it puts children's other rights at risk: non-discrimination, privacy, being heard, civil freedoms and remedy. Sets out how European policymakers, regulators and civil society could use age assurance in a child-rights-respecting way.
literature.summary_plain: Researchers from the LSE and Leiden University find that online age checks often fail to protect children and can harm their other rights.
literature.quality: Peer-reviewed; mixed legal and social research methods.
literature.verified: abstract read (Crossref doi:10.1163/15718182-32030001); Leiden University news page blocks automated reading
literature.citation: Livingstone, S., Nair, A., Stoilova, M., van der Hof, S. and Caglar, C. (2024), Children's Rights and Online Age Assurance Systems: The Way Forward, The International Journal of Children's Rights 32(3), 721–747, doi:10.1163/15718182-32030001
